listenings.text: Most conference openings waste their first thirty seconds, and they waste them in the same way. The speaker thanks the organizers, thanks the sponsors, reads the agenda and says his own name, which is already on the screen behind him. By the time he reaches an idea, half the room is reading email. The first thirty seconds are the only moment when every person in the hall is listening at the same time, so spend them on the one thing you want remembered. Then plan two more moments before you walk on stage: the turn, where you move from the good news to the hard question, and the handover, where you give the stage away cleanly. Thank the sponsors at the end. They will survive, and your audience will still be awake.

Good morning, and welcome. I am not going to read you the agenda; it is already in your hands. Instead, I would like a quick show of hands. How many of you have waited more than a year for a regulator to publish a date? Keep your hands up if that delay changed your investment decision. Now look around the room. Rarely do we have the people who waited and the people who made them wait in the same place, and this morning we do. Over the next ninety minutes we will talk about three things: contracts, currency and courage. One housekeeping note before we begin: the session ends at eleven sharp, because the minister has a flight to catch. With that, let me hand over to our first panelist.
